faq.q: Why is usable ZFS capacity less than raw drive manufacturer size?
faq.a: Drive manufacturers market drives using decimal terabytes (1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes), whereas ZFS and operating systems allocate space in binary tebibytes (1 TiB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes). Additionally, ZFS reserves ~3% slop space for internal metadata and copy-on-write overhead.

faq.q: Why is the 80% pool capacity rule important in ZFS?
faq.a: ZFS uses a copy-on-write transaction model. When a pool exceeds 80% capacity, the space allocator switches from first-fit to best-fit algorithms, resulting in severe write performance degradation and fragmentation.

faq.q: What is the minimum recommended drive count for RAIDZ2?
faq.a: While RAIDZ2 can function with 4 drives, 6 to 8 drives per vdev is standard engineering practice to balance parity overhead (33% to 25%) with high fault tolerance.

faq.q: When should I deploy a SLOG or L2ARC cache device?
faq.a: A dedicated SLOG (Separate ZFS Intent Log) device on high-write endurance NVMe is recommended for synchronous write workloads (NFS, databases, VM storage). L2ARC is recommended when your active working dataset exceeds physical RAM.

articleHtml:
OpenZFS Storage Pool Sizing & Redundancy Math

Designing a high-reliability Network Attached Storage (NAS) pool using OpenZFS or TrueNAS requires a thorough mathematical understanding of storage topology, binary tebibytes (TiB) versus decimal terabytes (TB), and copy-on-write allocation dynamics. Unlike legacy hardware RAID controllers that manage fixed logical units, ZFS integrates file system allocation directly with virtual storage device (vdev) pooling.

The most common planning surprise encountered by system administrators is the discrepancy between drive manufacturer packaging and operating system reporting. Storage disk manufacturers sell drives based on decimal SI units (1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes). However, operating system filesystems allocate storage using binary units (1 TiB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes). This creates an immediate ~9% mathematical reduction before accounting for parity disks, copy-on-write slop space reservations, or padding overhead.

VDEV Topology Engineering Guidelines

  • RAIDZ1 (Single Parity): Allocates one drive per vdev to parity. Can survive one drive failure. Recommended primarily for low-priority media libraries or SSD pools where resilver times are measured in minutes rather than days.
  • RAIDZ2 (Double Parity): Allocates two drives per vdev to parity. Can survive two simultaneous drive failures. Standard industry recommendation for enterprise hard drive arrays (exceeding 8 TB drive capacities) where high stress during rebuilds increases unrecoverable read error (URE) risks.
  • RAIDZ3 (Triple Parity): Allocates three drives per vdev to parity. Reserved for ultra-dense vdevs (12 to 16 drives) or archival tiers requiring extreme fault tolerance.
  • Mirrored VDEVs (RAID 10 equivalent): Drives are paired into 2-way mirror sets. Yields 50% capacity efficiency but provides superior random IOPS and the fastest possible resilver speeds with zero parity parity computation overhead.

The Critical 80% Pool Fill Threshold

ZFS allocates data blocks using a Copy-on-Write (CoW) transactional engine. When a pool is under 80% capacity, the space allocator utilizes a rapid first-fit strategy that minimizes latency. As pool utilization crosses 80%, the allocator automatically falls back to an exhaustive best-fit search across metaslabs to find contiguous free blocks. This shift induces catastrophic write performance degradation and persistent dataset fragmentation. TrueNAS and OpenZFS best practices mandate keeping pool utilization strictly below 80%.

Copy-on-Write Storage Architecture & VDEV Allocation

OpenZFS represents a fundamental departure from legacy filesystem and volume manager architectures. Traditional systems separate the volume manager (such as mdadm or hardware RAID) from the filesystem layer (such as ext4 or NTFS). In contrast, ZFS unifies volume management and storage pooling into a cohesive architecture.

Storage capacity is pooled across virtual devices (vdevs). In RAID-Z configurations, parity is computed dynamically on a per-block basis rather than using fixed stripe widths. This dynamic allocation eliminates the infamous "RAID 5 write hole" vulnerability without requiring battery-backed hardware RAID controllers. However, because ZFS writes new data to unallocated blocks before updating metadata pointers, maintaining adequate free storage space is critical for system stability.

Decimal TB vs Binary TiB Storage Mathematics

The disparity between marketed drive size and true binary capacity grows exponentially with drive scale:

Decimal Terabyte (TB) = 10^12 bytes = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes
Binary Tebibyte (TiB) = 2^40 bytes = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes
Conversion Factor = (10^12) / (2^40) = ~0.9094947

A 20 TB commercial hard drive yields approximately 18.19 TiB of raw binary space. In a 6-drive RAIDZ2 pool (4 data drives + 2 parity drives), the raw binary capacity is 72.76 TiB. After OpenZFS reserves ~3% slop space for transactional metadata and copy-on-write allocation buffers, the true usable capacity is approximately 70.6 TiB.

SLOG (ZIL) and L2ARC Cache Sizing Rules

For write-intensive workloads utilizing synchronous writes (such as NFS datastores for VMware or database transactions), deploying a dedicated Separate ZFS Intent Log (SLOG) device using enterprise NVMe drives with Power Loss Protection (PLP) drastically lowers latency. SLOG devices only need to buffer ~5 seconds of maximum network throughput (typically 16 GB to 32 GB). Meanwhile, L2ARC (Level 2 Adaptive Replacement Cache) using fast read SSDs extends RAM caching for high-concurrency read environments.
